passage:
Dear Ganga di,
You'll laugh at this. Our robotics team had to fill in a peer contribution form today, where each of us writes what percent of the work we did. I wrote 40%. Honestly, I thought I was being modest. I did the motor code and the wiring diagram, and I stayed back three evenings.
Then Prof. Iyer read the numbers aloud, without names. 40, 35, 40, 30. That's 145% of one robot.
Everyone went quiet. I'm sure Harpreet remembers her late nights on the chassis as clearly as I remember mine. I never saw her nights; she never saw mine.
Prof. Iyer said that from next week we keep a shared task log with dates. I grumbled, but I think it's fair.
Your brother,
Tushar

qa.q: What did the four contribution numbers add up to?
qa.a: They added up to 145% of one robot.

qa.q: Why did Tushar feel that writing 40% was modest?
qa.a: He clearly remembered his motor code, wiring diagram and three late evenings, while other people's hours were invisible to him.

qa.q: What will help the robotics team share credit fairly from now on?
qa.a: The shared task log with dates that Prof. Iyer asked for, so credit rests on records instead of memory.

qa.q: How might Harpreet see her own share of the robot?
qa.a: Harpreet probably remembers her late nights on the chassis just as vividly, so her own number feels right to her too.

grounding: A student realises every teammate claimed a big share of the work, adding to far over the whole, and accepts a written log.

passage: Chai stall, the night after our cultural fest. That's where it started, Sangeeta. I'm Lakshmi, and I ran the decoration team, five of us. We started saying who did what. I said I'd basically done the stage backdrop alone. Reuben said he'd done the backdrop. Farzana said she did the lights and most of the backdrop. Deepak said without his wooden frame there was no backdrop at all. We laughed, but it got tense. Each of us had been there for our own hours and missed everyone else's. Nobody was lying, exactly. This year, before we started, I made a shared sheet: every task, every name, every date, filled in the same day. Nobody argues now. Well, less.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi make before the team started this year?
qa.a: Lakshmi made a shared sheet with every task, every name, every date.

qa.q: Why did each person believe they had done most of the backdrop?
qa.a: Each of them felt proud of their own hours and missed everyone else's, so their own work felt like the biggest part of the backdrop.

qa.q: Why does the shared sheet help the team?
qa.a: Writing tasks, names and dates the same day replaces fuzzy memories, so credit is shared on facts and arguments shrink.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when the others claimed the backdrop?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt his wooden frame was being ignored, since in his mind there was no backdrop without it.

grounding: A student recalls every decoration team member claiming the backdrop, and fixing credit with a written task sheet.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I share a hostel room with Sunaina, so I heard every chapter of her group's market survey. Monday night she said, "I'm carrying this whole project. I made the questionnaire." On Tuesday her teammate Kunal dropped by for notes and told me, quietly, that he'd done basically all the data entry, "like 300 forms." On Wednesday, in the mess, Ishita said she'd written the whole report and the others had just helped. I don't know who really did what. Maybe all three were right about their own parts and blind to the rest. On Friday Sunaina came back upset: their guide had asked each of them to write down their share, and together it came to far more than the whole. She sat down with a blank page and started a list, with dates.

qa.q: How many forms did Kunal say he had entered?
qa.a: Kunal said he'd done basically all the data entry, like 300 forms.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina honestly feel she is carrying the whole project?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel stressed and proud of the questionnaire because she lived through every hour of making it, but saw little of Kunal's data entry or Ishita's writing. So her part looms largest.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina's list with dates a good next step?
qa.a: A dated list shows who did what as it happens, so the team can agree on shares instead of each trusting their own memory.

qa.q: How does Nandini see the three different claims?
qa.a: Nandini doesn't pick a side, and thinks all three may be right about their own parts and blind to the rest.

grounding: A roommate hears three teammates each claim most of a project, until their shares add up to more than the whole.

Week one. The street-play team of four met in the college canteen to split the work. Jagdish took the script. Preeti took costumes and permissions. Nobody wrote anything down. "We'll just remember," Jagdish said.
Week three. Rehearsals ran late every night. Jagdish rewrote scene two at 1 a.m. and thought, I'm basically carrying this. Across town, Preeti was stitching the last banner after getting the police permission stamped, thinking the exact same thing about herself.
Week five, the day after the performance. Their mentor asked each of them to write privately what share of the work they'd done. Jagdish wrote 50%. Preeti wrote 45%. The other two wrote 40% and 35%. The mentor added it up on the whiteboard: 170%. Everyone laughed, then went quiet. "Next time," Preeti said slowly, "we keep a shared task log. With dates."

qa.q: What did the four shares add up to on the whiteboard?
qa.a: They added up to 170%.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish feel like the one 'basically carrying' the play?
qa.a: Jagdish felt tired and overburdened, seeing every late night spent rewriting the script but not Preeti stitching banners or chasing permissions, so that work felt like most of it.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti suggest after the numbers were added, and why would it help?
qa.a: She suggested a shared task log with dates, so next time everyone's work is visible on paper instead of each person remembering mostly their own.

qa.q: How might the other two members have felt when the mentor wrote 170%?
qa.a: They may have been amused and then uncomfortable, realising they too had quietly believed their own share was bigger than the others could see.

grounding: Across three beats it shows every member of a college team quietly counting their own work as most of it, until the shares add up to far more than the whole.

passage:
Chetan, before you fill in that peer-rating form, sit a minute. Let me, Saurabh, your old senior on this floor, tell you about my final-year engineering project, back in 2009.
There were five of us building a water-level sensor. I was sure I had done the real work: I wrote the code, stayed up the night before the demo. Deepak thought the same about his circuit board. Farida thought she had saved us all by writing the report. Nitin believed his contacts got us the lab slot.
Our professor made each of us write our share on a slip. Mine said 40%. When she read them out, the total was nearly double a hundred. I remember my ears going hot.
She said, "Every one of you is honest, and every one of you is wrong." After that we kept a diary of who did what, every day, signed by all five. It saved friendships.

qa.q: What were the five students in Saurabh's team building?
qa.a: They were building a water-level sensor.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh so sure of having done the real work?
qa.a: Saurabh felt proud of the code and the all-nighter before the demo, which were remembered clearly, while the others' efforts were less visible, so that part felt biggest.

qa.q: What did the team start doing after the slips were read out, and why did it matter?
qa.a: They kept a daily diary of who did what, signed by all five, so credit rested on a written record rather than on each person's memory, which kept friendships intact.

qa.q: How might Chetan look at the peer-rating form after hearing the story?
qa.a: Chetan may realise that a personal sense of doing most of the work could feel just as true and be just as off, and might check notes or ask teammates before rating.

grounding: A senior recalls a college project where each member honestly believed their own share was the biggest, and a written daily record fixed it.

passage: At the end of our marketing project, our professor did something sneaky. She asked each of the four of us, privately, to write what percentage of the work we had done. I wrote 45%, and honestly I thought I was being modest. I had stayed up all night for the final deck. Then she read out the numbers. Zeenat, 40%. Kiran, 50%. Tushar, 55%. Me, 45%. Each of us had seen our own late nights up close and everyone else's from far away. On the next project, we kept a shared log of who did what, with dates.

passage:
Project guide's note, final-year mechanical projects, 20 April
During today's viva, Thomas and Uday each told me separately that they had built most of the solar dryer. Thomas said he "did the whole frame and all the calculations." Uday said he "designed it and handled the frame welding." Both were sincere; neither was lying on purpose. When I asked for their work logs, they had none. From the photos on their phones, it looks as though Thomas did most of the calculations and Uday most of the welding, and each remembers his own part as the bigger one. I have asked both to write a dated list of tasks from their messages and photos before marks are finalised. From next year, I will ask every team to keep a weekly log from day one.

qa.q: What did Thomas say he did?
qa.a: The whole frame and all the calculations.

qa.q: Why might Thomas and Uday both sincerely believe they did most of the work?
qa.a: Each felt proud of his own long hours, which he remembers up close, while the other's work seemed smaller from a distance.

qa.q: What is the guide asking for, and why is it fair?
qa.a: A dated task list from messages and photos, and weekly logs next year, so recognition rests on records rather than memory.

qa.q: How might Uday feel when he hears Thomas's claim?
qa.a: Uday might feel hurt or annoyed, since he remembers designing it and doing the welding himself.

grounding: A project guide records two students each sincerely claiming most of the work, and asks for dated records to settle credit.

passage:
Friday, hostel
Presentation done. We got an A. And honestly? That was mostly me. I did the research, the slides AND I presented. Uday just did "the data," whatever that was.
Later, in the mess, I heard Uday tell Nitin he had "carried the whole thing," because he spent three nights cleaning the survey data. Three nights? I didn't even know that took three nights. I was annoyed at first. Then I tried adding it up: if he thinks he did 70% and I think I did 70%, that's 140%. We can't both be right.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask him to go through our chat history with me and write down who did what. Next time, a shared list from day one.
Sachin

qa.a: Three nights.

qa.a: Sachin felt annoyed at first, then uneasy on realising they both believed they had done most of the work.

qa.q: What does Sachin plan, and why could it help?

passage: The polytechnic in Hosur had given its prize for the best working model to Anand's team: a small solar pump that lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot. That evening the principal called each of the three boys in, one by one, to write a line for the college newsletter about who did what. Anand said he had designed the pump and done "most of it." Kamal said he had wired the solar panel and fixed the leaks, "which was really the hard part." The third boy said the pump would never have run without his gearbox. The principal smiled and opened the lab register, where each boy signed in and out and wrote what he worked on. Anand's signature was there on eleven days. Kamal's on fourteen. The third boy's on twelve. Nobody had done most of it.

passage: The peer-evaluation forms for the marketing project at the university in Leeds were due by midnight. Emeka filled his in the library café: "My share of the work: 45%. I set up every meeting and wrote the pitch." Across town, Wei typed: "My share: 50%. I built the survey and ran all the numbers." Their third teammate, a quiet student from Poland, wrote 40%. The tutor, reading them the next day, added the numbers on a sticky note and called all three in. "You've done 135% of one project," she said. Emeka laughed, then stopped. He really had believed his number. So had Wei. The tutor handed them a blank task sheet. "Next time, you each log your hours as you go. I'll mark from this." Wei looked at Emeka. "I didn't know you did all the meeting notes." "I didn't know about the survey weekends."

The robotics lab at the engineering college smelled of solder. The team had just won second place at the state contest, and Professor Nair asked each of the four members to write, privately, what share of the work they had done.

Pradeep wrote 50%. He'd built the arm. Bhupen wrote 45%. He'd written the code. The other two wrote 40% and 35%.

The professor added them up on the whiteboard. "One hundred and seventy percent. Interesting robot."

Everyone laughed, a bit awkwardly. Pradeep felt a flash of annoyance. Surely his share was obvious? Then he remembered the nights Bhupen had stayed till two debugging, which Pradeep had been asleep for.

"You each remember your own late nights very clearly," the professor said. "Other people's, less so."

For the next project, she handed them a shared logbook. "Write what you did, every day. Then we'll talk about credit."

qa.q: What did the four shares add up to?
qa.a: One hundred and seventy percent.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when the total went on the board?
qa.a: Pradeep felt a flash of annoyance, sure his share was obvious, then a little sheepish remembering Bhupen's late nights.

qa.q: Why is the professor's shared logbook a good fix?
qa.a: A written daily record shows everyone's work, not just what each person remembers of their own, so credit is fairer.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Pradeep's 50%?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel his debugging nights were overlooked, since his own memory of that work is vivid too.

grounding: Each member of a college robotics team thinks he did most of the work, and the shares add up to far more than the whole.

passage:
Dear Raghav,

I've been thinking about the argument after our marketing project presentation, and I owe you a proper message.

When the professor asked who led the project, I said I did. You looked hurt. I was annoyed that you looked hurt. In my head, I'd done most of it: the research, the slides, the late calls.

Then last night I went back through our chat history, from week one. You'd drafted the survey. You'd done all the data cleaning. You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight. I honestly didn't remember most of it.

I remembered my work because I was tired while doing it. Yours happened while I was asleep or busy.

I think if we'd both written down what we did each week, neither of us would have been so sure. Can we do that for the next project? And I'm sorry.

Eshaan

qa.q: What did Raghav do at midnight?
qa.a: You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when Raghav looked hurt?
qa.a: Eshaan felt annoyed at first, sure of having done most of the work, and later felt sorry after checking the chat.

qa.q: What does Eshaan propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Eshaan proposes writing down what each person does every week, so credit rests on a record instead of memory.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Raghav might feel relieved and respected that Eshaan checked the record and apologised.

grounding: A student who claimed to have led a project checks the chat history and sees a teammate's share, proposing written records.

passage:
You asked why our hackathon team split up, Gautam? I'm Yusuf. Let me tell you what I learned.

We were three: me, Dev and Kunal. We built a bus-tracking app in thirty-six hours and won. On the train home, someone asked who did most of it. I said, "Honestly, I did about half." Dev said he'd done half. Kunal said he'd done half.

That's a hundred and fifty percent.

We argued all the way to Pune. Each of us could list everything we'd done in detail. I remembered every bug I fixed. I barely remembered Kunal's design work, though it was the reason the judges liked it.

We stopped talking for a month.

Now, on every team, I keep a shared sheet from day one: who did what, each day. It's boring. But when credit comes, nobody has to argue from memory.

qa.q: What app did Yusuf's team build?
qa.a: A bus-tracking app.

qa.q: Why was Yusuf so sure of having done about half?
qa.a: Yusuf felt proud and certain because every bug Yusuf fixed was vivid in memory, while Kunal's design work barely registered.

qa.q: What habit does Yusuf now keep, and why does it help?
qa.a: Yusuf keeps a shared sheet of who did what each day, so credit is based on a record rather than each person's memory.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when his design work was overlooked?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt hurt and underappreciated, since his design was why the judges liked the app.

grounding: Each member of a hackathon team claims about half the work, and only a written record could settle it.
